questions.prompt: G2 BRIEF — javabootcamp (System Design block; guide astraupskill/03-SYSTEM-DESIGN.md). You will delegate a design task to a coding agent: a written design for a parking-lot reservation system, one of the unseen designs the guide suggests practising, which you will review before anyone writes code. Write the brief: goal and deliverable, what the agent must read, boundaries, how you will verify the result, stop condition. Commit to your brief first, then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Goal and deliverable: one design document that walks the guide's eight steps in order (scope, qualities, estimate, interface, data, sketch, deep dive, failure), each with its stated output.

[w3] Requirements first and written down: the agent records what must hold (for example 'a spot is reserved by at most one driver') and what may be stale, because those answers decide the storage choices.
[w2] Numbers are mandatory: a back-of-the-envelope estimate (peak QPS, storage per year) even though nobody asked for one.
[w2] Inputs named: the guide plus the module READMEs 09-13, and every box in the sketch labelled with the exercise that built it.
keyPoints.quote: label every box with the exercise that built it

keyPoints.text: [w3] Boundary: design only, no code; the agent does not open bootcamp/*/solutions/, which the learner reads only after their own exercise is green.
[w2] Boundary: access patterns before technology; no 'we will use Kafka and Cassandra' before the read/write ratio is known.
[w2] The happy path is drawn first, one request end to end, and only then attacked (100 times bigger, a slow box, a duplicate message).
[w2] Stop condition: done when the failure step names every single point of failure and what happens when it dies; questions the requirements do not answer are handed back, not invented.

questions.prompt: G2 PRE-MORTEM — same delegation. What are the likeliest ways the agent's design goes wrong, and what line of your brief prevents each?

keyPoints.text: [w3] It promises 'exactly once' for reservations instead of at-least-once plus idempotent consumers, without saying where the dedupe state lives or how long it is kept.
[w3] It adds retries everywhere with idempotency nowhere, so a retried 'reserve' or 'pay' can happen twice.
[w2] It puts a cache in front of availability without a sentence on invalidation or an acceptable staleness number.
[w2] It expires reservations by comparing wall-clock times across machines instead of leases with margins, fencing tokens or a single ordering authority.
[w2] It over-engineers: shards a dataset that fits on one machine and gives up joins and transactions without showing the number that forces it.
[w1] It forgets deletes: cancelled reservations must invalidate caches, leave tombstones or compensating events, and never reuse ids.

questions.prompt: G2 HANDBACK REVIEW — the agent hands back the design document and says it is complete. What do you check before you accept it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] Every added box says which side of its trade the requirements chose: cache latency vs staleness, queue decoupling vs ordering, replica availability vs consistency.
[w3] The deep dive names where the design breaks first and gives the fix together with its trade-off, rather than a list of components.
[w2] Each trade-off appears as one row of the guide's tables, stating the column chosen and why.
[w2] Re-do the envelope arithmetic yourself: requests a day divided by about 10^5 gives per second, then 2-3x for peak.
[w2] The failure step covers each box dying or slowing down: timeouts, retries, idempotency and degradation.
[w1] The handback changed no repository files: nothing under exercises/ or solutions/ was touched or quoted.
